lesson.title: Donner, Bad & Du
lesson.subtitle: thunder-day, bath towns, and the thou you already speak

hook.title: Thor Kept His Day, Lost His Name
hook.content: English named Thursday after the thunder god Thor — Thor's day. German named the same day after the god's weapon: Donner (thunder) + Tag (day) = Donnerstag. Two languages, one god, one shift: his English name kept the TH his German audience hardened into D. And the D's keep coming: Bad (bath) gave Germany its spa towns — Baden-Baden literally says 'bath-bath'. Du is thou — same word, same ancient -st verb ending (thou hast ↔ du hast).

footnotes.title: The Reindeer Spell It Out
footnotes.content: Santa's reindeer 'Donner and Blitzen' are simply Thunder and Lightning — the German words, kept alive in English pop culture since the 1823 poem. Donnerstag means Thunder-day; Blitzen means lightning.

pattern.title: Culture Words Through the D-Lens
pattern.content: The TH → D shift is not just body parts and function words — it runs through culture. Thunder → Donner, bath → Bad (the verb is baden, 'to bathe'; final -d is pronounced [t]: Bad sounds like 'baht'), thou → du with thee → dich/dir. And the think/thank pair shines again: danken (to thank) is just 'a good thought' spoken aloud — ich danke dir, I thank thee. Three, drei, counts itself.
pattern.linguist_note: German weekday names are a cultural fossil map: Donnerstag (Thunder's day) kept Thor's element where English kept Thor's name. Mittwoch replaced Woden with 'mid-week' — the one weekday that broke the god-name pattern entirely.

exercises.prompt: Match the words through the TH → D lens — the culture set, plus three everyday arrivals:
exercises.target_answer: Donner, Bad, du, danken, Mund, Monat, Darm
exercises.meaning: thunder, bath, thou, to thank, mouth, month, gut
exercises.explanation: Every German d here answers to an English th — including the god of thunder himself. Darm is the old tharm: English moved to 'gut', German kept the hardened th.

exercises.prompt: Donnerstag hides two shifted words — which English weekday is its twin?
exercises.explanation: English kept the god (Thor), German kept his weapon (Donner). Same day, same god, one shift.

exercises.prompt: German 'Bad' is written with a final -d but sounds like 'baht'. Why?
options: German devoices final consonants: written -d is pronounced [t]
It is a spelling mistake in German
exercises.target_answer: German devoices final consonants: written -d is pronounced [t]
exercises.explanation: Final d hardens to [t] in speech — the same habit that keeps gut and kalt crisp at the end, just as PF- keeps Pfirsich and Pflanze crisp at the start.

exercises.prompt: Complete with the du-form of haben: 'Du _____ einen Bruder' (you have):
exercises.explanation: du hast keeps the same -st ending Early Modern English wrote as -est in 'thou hast'.

exercises.idea: someone just helped you, and you want to thank them personally: I thank thee
cues: Who thanks? → ich danke (thank with TH → D)
German thanks TO a person: danke + dir
dir is the 'to thee' form of du — the thanks travel TO someone
exercises.meaning: I thank thee / I thank you

vocab_hints.note: danken takes the dative: you thank someone (jemandem danken) — dir is the dative 'to thee' form of du

exercises.explanation: ich danke dir — German thanks TO a person, the same dative logic as archaic English 'I give it thee'.

summary.outcome: Use the cultural TH→D words: thunder-day, bath, thou — and say what you like in German.
summary.takeaway: German culture words carry the shift: Donner = thunder, Bad = bath, du = thou — and final -d sounds like [t].
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: cross-shift drills — separate the true TH→D words from the D→T impostors.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Donner, Bad & Du (I thank thee / I thank you):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Ich danke dir" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Donner, Bad & Du without relying on short-term echo.

donner.etymology_derivation: TH → D hardening. Living in English "Thursday" (Thor's/Thunder's day = Donnerstag) and Santa's reindeer "Donner and Blitzen" (Thunder and Lightning).

bad.etymology_derivation: Final th shifted to d (devoiced in pronunciation to [t]). Verb: baden (to bathe).

du.etymology_derivation: Direct cognate of archaic English "thou". Conjugates with -st (thou goest ↔ du gehst).

danken.etymology_derivation: Danke is an ellipsis of "[Ich] danke [dir/Ihnen]".

denken.etymology_derivation: TH → D hardening. Shares the exact vowel-shift relationship with "danken" that English has in "think" and "thank" (a thank is a good thought).

bruder.etymology_derivation: Medial th shifted to d; unstressed -er vocalizes to [ɐ].

mund.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *munþaz — English kept the th, German hardened it to d. [wiktionary]

kleid.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *klaiþą — English cloth is the cognate: English th ↔ German d. [wiktionary]

monat.etymology_derivation: The twin of English month, from *mānōþ 'moon' (see der Mond) — th→d included. [wiktionary]

darm.context_phrase: Der Magen und der Darm verdauen das Essen.
darm.context_translation: The stomach and the intestine digest the food.

pfirsich.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic persik, from Late Latin persicum, meaning Persian apple; English peach descends from the same Latin word, with p corresponding to German pf. [wiktionary]

pflanze.shift_rule: P → PF / F + T → S / SS / Z
pflanze.etymology_derivation: Double shift: initial p → pf and t → z [ts].

noch.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *nuh, from PIE *nu 'now' plus *-kʷe 'and, also' — literally and-now; the page lists no English cognate, but that first piece is the very 'now' element. [wiktionary]

kostenlos.etymology_derivation: Kosten (costs) + -los (free of); the page itself compares English costless — free of cost. [wiktionary]

diebstahl.context_phrase: Die Polizei meldet einen Diebstahl im Laden.
diebstahl.context_translation: The police report a theft in the shop.
diebstahl.etymology_derivation: Dieb + Stahl, a noun from stehlen: Dieb is the documented twin of thief (th to d, f to b) and stehlen the twin of steal — the German parallel to English theft. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops. This gives you an instant key to dozens of core words.
th_to_d.literature_source: Documented in Joseph Wright's Historical German Grammar as the primary dental hardening of the Second Sound Shift.
